screens.title: C Programming Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Why C matters for embedded systems and the key building blocks you'll use every day

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on C as the practical language of embedded systems. You will learn why C is commonly chosen for microcontrollers: it compiles to native instructions, gives predictable performance, and lets you control hardware at the register and bit level. We'll walk through the minimal structure of an embedded program, the persistent main loop that runs forever, and the fixed-width integer types from the standard header that make behavior portable across devices. You will also practice operators that let you manipulate values and bits, and control structures that steer program flow in response to sensors and events. Throughout, we will highlight common pitfalls, like integer overflow, and show simple ways to avoid them by choosing the right type and adding checks. By the end of the lesson you will understand how to write a readable, well-structured C program for an ARM Cortex-M target, how to choose fixed-width types such as uint8_t and uint32_t, and how to reason about loop behavior and bit operations. Think of this chapter as the essential toolkit you will reach for whenever you write firmware.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: C gives efficient, predictable control over microcontrollers; use fixed-width types and a simple infinite main loop to build reliable firmware.

C Programming Fundamentals

This lesson shows you how to write simple, reliable firmware: the minimal program structure, data types that guarantee size, primary operators, and key control structures used in embedded code.

In this lesson
Write and run a basic loop-based program and choose fixed-width types for portability.
Key idea
C compiles to native code; use stdint.h types to avoid surprises across platforms.
Hands-on
Count 0 to 255 with a uint8_t and watch wrap-around behavior in the debugger.
Explore Key Topics
Program Structure
main() as the entry, and an infinite loop that keeps the microcontroller running.
Fixed-width Types
Use uint8_t, int16_t, uint32_t for predictable sizes and behavior across toolchains.
Control & Operators
If, for, switch, and bitwise operators are the building blocks of firmware logic and register control.
Code snapshot
Live coding view
#include <stdint.h>

int main(void) {
    uint32_t counter = 0;
    while (1) {
        counter = counter + 1;
        // sensor read, decision, output update
    }
}
Why this matters
Understanding these basics makes firmware predictable and debuggable. Small choices like type width have system-level effects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll practice and why they matter for firmware development

narration.text: Over the next screens you will practice four primary skills. First, you will write and compile simple C programs targeted at the ARM Cortex-M processor and see how the compiled code runs in a persistent main loop. This shows you how firmware starts and continues running. Second, you will use variables, data types, operators, and control structures to implement logic and state in your program. These are the grammar of firmware code. Third, you will learn the practical difference between signed and unsigned integers and why fixed-width types from the standard header are essential for portability. This prevents surprises when your code moves between toolchains. Fourth, you will structure programs with clear comments and formatting so others — and your future self — can read and maintain firmware. Each objective includes a brief task and an example that you can test in a simulator or debugger. These skills together let you write efficient, predictable embedded code for real microcontrollers.

screens.title: Why C is the language of embedded systems
screens.subtitle: Efficiency, predictability, and hardware control

narration.text: C is widely used in embedded systems because it balances low-level access with concise, portable syntax. When you write C and compile for a microcontroller, the compiler emits native instructions that execute directly on the processor core. That direct mapping gives two important advantages: speed and predictability. Speed matters when your loop must respond to an interrupt or meet a timing deadline. Predictability matters because many embedded applications are real-time and must behave reliably. C also exposes the memory model and allows direct manipulation of hardware registers and bits, which higher-level languages usually abstract away. A concrete example is toggling a GPIO pin: in C you can write to a register using bitwise operations to change only the bit you need, leaving other bits untouched. A common misconception is that C is unsafe by default — while it does give more control, careful type selection, clear comments, and consistent patterns make C code both safe and understandable. The takeaway is that C's low-level control is what allows efficient, deterministic firmware, but that control demands disciplined coding practices. Why C is the language of embedded systems means c provides direct hardware access and predictable native performance, which are essential properties for embedded firmware.. In practical terms, efficiency, predictability, and hardware control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition

C compiles to native code, offers direct access to memory and registers, and supports compact, efficient programs suitable for resource-constrained microcontrollers.

Toggling a pin by writing a value to a register and using bitwise operations to change only specific bits without disturbing others.

Key Takeaway

C's low-level capabilities make it ideal for firmware, but they require disciplined type choices and clear code to remain reliable.

Analogy

Think of C as the instrument panel controls in a machine: it gives you direct knobs and switches rather than higher-level automated menus. That directness is powerful if you know how to use it responsibly.

Why this matters

  • Explicit memory access enables precise control of peripherals and DMA.
  • Predictable behavior simplifies reasoning about timing and resource use.

screens.title: The minimal embedded C program
screens.subtitle: main(), initialization, and the infinite while loop

narration.text: A minimal embedded program has three parts: headers that bring in fixed-width types, initialization code that runs once, and an infinite main loop that performs ongoing tasks. The program begins at main, which on a microcontroller typically initializes hardware and then enters an endless while loop. That loop repeatedly reads sensors, makes decisions, and updates outputs until power is removed. A familiar snippet shows this structure: you include the header that defines uint32_t, declare and initialize variables, and then write while(1) to create a loop that never exits. The initialization section is important because it sets pin directions, peripheral clocks, and initial state; if initialization is incomplete, the system may behave unpredictably. A common misconception is expecting main to return like a desktop program — embedded main intentionally does not return because the device is intended to run continuously. In practice your loop may call lower-level handlers or sleep between cycles to save power. Think about what must run once versus what must run continuously when you design firmware. The minimal embedded C program means use initialization once at startup, then a perpetual main loop for repeated tasks; main does not return on an embedded device.. In practical terms, main(), initialization, and the infinite while loop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Program form
keyIdea.text: Use initialization once at startup, then a perpetual main loop for repeated tasks; main does not return on an embedded device.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › The minimal embedded C program
Code walkthrough
#include <stdint.h>

int main(void) {
    // Initialization runs once
    uint32_t counter = 0;

    // Infinite loop runs forever
    while (1) {
        counter = counter + 1;
        // sensor read, decision, output update
    }
}
Initialization
Set up clocks, configure pin directions, initialize peripherals. This code runs just once at startup.
Main loop
The perpetual loop handles sensing and actuation. It does not return on embedded systems.
Check your understanding

Why must initialization run once, and what could happen if you reinitialize a peripheral inside the main loop by mistake?

Common mistake
Reinitializing peripherals inside the loop may reset settings, drop data, or disrupt timing. Keep one-time setup in initialization and repeated tasks in the loop.
Key Takeaway
Separate startup configuration from periodic work. Treat main as the perpetual runtime environment of your device.

screens.title: Fixed-width integer types from stdint.h
screens.subtitle: Why uint8_t, int16_t, and uint32_t make firmware portable

narration.text: In embedded programming we prefer fixed-width types because they explicitly state how many bits a variable uses. The standard header provides types such as uint8_t for unsigned eight-bit values, int16_t for signed sixteen-bit values, and uint32_t for unsigned thirty-two-bit values. These names tell you the exact size and signedness, which avoids ambiguous assumptions about types like int or long that can vary by compiler and target. For instance, on an ARM Cortex-M4 a plain int is typically 32 bits, but on an older 8-bit microcontroller an int might be 16 bits. Using uint32_t guarantees the same size everywhere, which prevents bugs when code is ported between boards. A concrete example: a sensor that reports a value up to 65,000 should use uint16_t to hold the full range reliably. A common misconception is that fixed-width types are only for advanced code; in fact they are a basic defensive practice that reduces bugs and makes your intent explicit. The takeaway: choose the narrowest type that fits your required range, and prefer explicit fixed-width types for clarity and portability. Fixed-width integer types from stdint.h means use stdint.h types to guarantee size and signedness, preventing portability surprises and enabling precise range reasoning.. In practical terms, why uint8_t, int16_t, and uint32_t make firmware portable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fixed-width types

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Fixed-width integer types
Type reference
  • uint8_t — unsigned 8-bit integer (0 to 255)
  • int8_t — signed 8-bit integer (-128 to 127)
  • uint16_t — unsigned 16-bit integer (0 to 65,535)
  • int16_t — signed 16-bit integer (-32,768 to 32,767)
  • uint32_t / int32_t — unsigned/signed 32-bit integers
Concrete scenario
If a sensor yields values up to 65,000, use uint16_t. Choosing uint8_t would overflow; choosing uint32_t wastes memory if many such variables exist.
Why portability matters

Different compilers and boards define plain types differently. Fixed-width names remove ambiguity and make code behavior consistent across targets.

Pitfall
Assuming an int is always 32 bits can lead to subtle bugs when moving code to smaller architectures. Always pick an explicit width when hardware constraints matter.
Key Takeaway
Prefer the narrowest fixed-width type that safely holds your range to balance memory use and correctness.

narration.text: Signed and unsigned integers differ in how the same bit pattern is interpreted. An unsigned eight-bit variable holds values from zero up to 255. The same eight bits interpreted as a signed int8_t represent negative values using two's complement, ranging from -128 to 127. This distinction matters when you mix types in expressions or when you choose a variable to hold sensor data, counters, or computed differences. A typical trap is subtracting two unsigned values and getting a very large positive number due to wrap-around when the result would be negative. For example, if you subtract a larger unsigned value from a smaller one, the result underflows and produces a high value instead of a negative. Concrete guidance: use unsigned types for counters and quantities that are never negative, and signed types for measurements that can go below zero. When combining different widths or signs in expressions, prefer casting intentionally and documenting your choice to avoid surprising implicit conversions. The learner question to close: which type would you choose for a temperature sensor that can be negative? Signed vs Unsigned integers means use unsigned for always-nonnegative counts, signed for values that may be negative, and be mindful of implicit conversions and underflow.. In practical terms, ranges, interpretations, and common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Signedness matters
keyIdea.text: Use unsigned for always-nonnegative counts, signed for values that may be negative, and be mindful of implicit conversions and underflow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Signed vs Unsigned integers
Comparison: ranges
uint8_t
0 to 255 — ideal for counters and indices that never go negative.
int8_t
-128 to 127 — use when values can be below zero, such as signed sensor offsets.
Example pitfall
Subtracting larger unsigned from smaller unsigned underflows and yields a large positive value because the result wraps around the maximum representable value.
Practical guidance
  • Use unsigned for nonnegative counts, sizes, and bit masks.
  • Use signed for signed measurements or differences that can be negative.
  • Cast explicitly when mixing signed and unsigned to show intent.
Common mistake
Assuming subtraction yields a negative signed result when variables are unsigned. This leads to surprising large values due to wrap-around.
Key Takeaway
Pick signedness to match the domain of the value and be explicit about conversions to avoid implicit, dangerous behavior.

screens.title: Operators with emphasis on bitwise operations
screens.subtitle: Arithmetic, logical, and bitwise operators you use in firmware

narration.text: Operators let you compute values, test conditions, and manipulate bits. Arithmetic operators such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus handle numeric calculations. Comparison operators check equality and ordering, and logical operators combine boolean conditions. Bitwise operators — AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and the left and right shifts — are particularly important in embedded systems. They let you set, clear, and toggle individual bits inside a hardware register or a flag variable without affecting other bits. For example, to set bit three you OR the register with a mask that has bit three set. To clear a bit you AND with the complement of the mask. A common misuse is applying arithmetic operations to registers without masking, which may change unintended bits. A concrete example is reading a status register, masking the bits you care about, and then testing the masked result for a condition. The final rule: use clear masks, name your masks with constants, and comment why each bit manipulation is performed so future maintainers understand the hardware intent. Operators with emphasis on bitwise operations means use bitwise operators to safely manipulate single bits in registers and flags; always use masks and document intent.. In practical terms, arithmetic, logical, and bitwise operators you use in firmware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bitwise importance
keyIdea.text: Use bitwise operators to safely manipulate single bits in registers and flags; always use masks and document intent.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Operators — bitwise emphasis
Operator categories
  • Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, % — numerical maths.
  • Comparison: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= — tests for decisions.
  • Logical: &&, ||, ! — combine boolean conditions.
  • Bitwise: &, |, ^, ~, <<, >> — manipulate individual bits.
Concrete example
Use a mask to set bit 3: perform register = register | (1u << 3). To clear bit 3: register = register & ~(1u << 3). Always use parenthesized masks to avoid precedence mistakes.
Common mistake
Applying arithmetic modification to a register without masking can change reserved bits and disrupt hardware state. Always mask and document which bits are safe to modify.
Pro tip
Define named constants for masks, like LED_MASK = (1u << 2), and use them to make intent clear.
Key Takeaway
Bitwise ops are the correct tool to change single bits; always use masks and named constants to prevent unintended side effects.

screens.title: Control structures: if, for, while
screens.subtitle: How firmware decides and repeats tasks

narration.text: Control structures let your firmware make choices and repeat actions. The if statement evaluates a condition and executes a block only when the condition is true, which is ideal for event-driven responses. For loops are used when you know how many iterations are needed, like initializing an array or toggling a set number of pins. While loops provide repeated behavior based on a condition and are often used for background tasks that continue until a sensor or flag changes. In embedded code the main loop itself is an infinite while construct that runs until power removal. A concrete example: use if to test a button press and change state, a for loop to scan a fixed number of ADC channels, and while to wait for a peripheral to signal readiness. A common pitfall is writing blocking loops that wait without returning control to other tasks; prefer non-blocking patterns or brief sleeps if the platform supports them. The takeaway: match the structure to the problem — deterministic repeats with for, event checks with if, and continuous operation with while. Control structures: if, for, while means use if for conditional decisions, for for counted repetition, and while for ongoing or conditional repetition; avoid blocking waits in critical real-time paths.. In practical terms, how firmware decides and repeats tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Control structures
keyIdea.text: Use if for conditional decisions, for for counted repetition, and while for ongoing or conditional repetition; avoid blocking waits in critical real-time paths.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Control structures: if, for, while
Process: choosing the right loop
if
Use for event-driven decisions, e.g., if a button is pressed then change state.
for
Use when the iteration count is known, like scanning a fixed array of sensors.
while
Use for repeated behavior until a condition changes, or the main runtime loop.
Concrete example
Inside main's infinite loop, poll a sensor with if for threshold crossings, use for to sample N channels, and use while carefully to wait for quick hardware readiness, avoiding long blocking delays.
Common mistake
Blocking waits in the main loop can prevent timely responses. Prefer brief non-blocking checks or state machines when responsiveness matters.
Key Takeaway
Match control structures to tasks: counted loops for fixed iterations, conditional checks for events, ongoing loops for continuous operation while avoiding long blocking calls.

screens.title: Using switch for state handling
screens.subtitle: Simplifying multi-way decisions and state machines

narration.text: The switch statement is useful when one variable can take many constant values and you want different behavior for each. In embedded systems it's a natural fit for simple state machines: map states to numbered cases and implement the actions associated with each state. Each case should end with a break to prevent fall-through unless fall-through is intentional and documented. A concrete scenario is handling operational modes: case 0 may mean idle, case 1 means sampling, case 2 means transmitting, and the default case handles unexpected states. This structure gives readable logic and makes it easy to add or remove states. Beware of forgetting break statements, which causes fall-through and unexpected execution of subsequent cases. Also avoid large switch blocks with complex logic in each case; instead call small helper functions or handlers for each state to preserve readability and testability. The learner should practice designing a simple state machine with at least three states mapped to cases and a default fallback for robustness. Using switch for state handling means use switch to map discrete states to actions; always include a default and avoid accidental fall-through by using breaks or documented fall-through with comments.. In practical terms, simplifying multi-way decisions and state machines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Switch & states
keyIdea.text: Use switch to map discrete states to actions; always include a default and avoid accidental fall-through by using breaks or documented fall-through with comments.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Using switch for state handling
Process: state machine with switch
Define an enum or integer for states and use switch to dispatch behavior. Keep each case small and call helper functions to keep logic clear and testable.
Example structure
state variable: 0 = idle, 1 = sample, 2 = transmit. In main loop, switch(state) handles each mode and updates state when transitions are needed. default handles unexpected states by resetting or logging.
Common mistake
Omitting break leads to fall-through. Only use fall-through intentionally and document it with a comment so future readers understand the intent.
Key Takeaway
Switch simplifies multi-way branching for state machines; include a default and keep case bodies concise by calling handlers.

screens.title: Overflow and wrap-around with fixed-width integers
screens.subtitle: Why adding values can produce surprising results

narration.text: Integer overflow occurs when a calculation produces a value outside the representable range of the chosen type. In fixed-width unsigned types, overflow wraps around modulo 2^N. A concrete example shows why this matters in firmware: start with uint8_t a = 250; uint8_t b = 20; then compute uint8_t c = a + b. The arithmetic sum is 270, but uint8_t can only hold 0 to 255, so the stored result wraps to 14. This wrap-around can silently corrupt counters, buffer indexes, or sensor calculations if not anticipated. Signed overflow is undefined behavior in C, which can lead to unpredictable results, so avoid relying on signed overflow for logic. Practical defenses include choosing a wider type for intermediate results, checking before arithmetic that the operation would overflow, or using saturation arithmetic where appropriate. A useful rule of thumb is to pick the smallest type that safely contains all possible intermediate values, not only the final range. Ask yourself: could any addition or multiplication temporarily exceed the storage size? If yes, use a larger intermediate type or add checks. Overflow and wrap-around with fixed-width integers means unsigned overflow wraps around; signed overflow is undefined. prevent errors by selecting appropriate widths or checking for overflow before operations.. In practical terms, why adding values can produce surprising results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Overflow effect
keyIdea.text: Unsigned overflow wraps around; signed overflow is undefined. Prevent errors by selecting appropriate widths or checking for overflow before operations.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Overflow and wrap-around
Concrete example
uint8_t a = 250;
uint8_t b = 20;
uint8_t c = a + b; // c == 14 due to wrap-around
This demonstrates unsigned wrap-around: the sum exceeds 255 and wraps modulo 256. In firmware, such wrap-around can silently corrupt logic like counters or buffer indices.
Defensive patterns
  • Use a wider intermediate type for calculations.
  • Check for overflow before performing arithmetic.
  • Use saturation arithmetic if wrap-around is unacceptable.
Why this is dangerous
Wrap-around often goes unnoticed in embedded systems because there is no runtime trap, which can lead to wrong actuator commands or corrupted counters.
Key Takeaway
Anticipate ranges and use types or checks that prevent silent overflow; treat signed overflow as undefined and avoid relying on it.

screens.title: Counting 0 to 255 with uint8_t
screens.subtitle: A simple lab to observe wrap-around and practice the main loop

narration.text: This hands-on exercise reinforces types and the main loop. Implement a variable declared as uint8_t and increment it inside the perpetual main loop. Because uint8_t holds 0 to 255, when the counter reaches 255 and you increment it the value wraps to 0. Observe the value either by printing over a serial interface or by watching it in the debugger. Add a small delay between increments to make the count visible. This lab teaches three practical points: the use of a fixed-width type, the behavior of wrap-around in unsigned arithmetic, and how to structure repeated work inside the infinite loop. A common extension is to add a conditional that triggers an LED toggle when the counter wraps to zero, demonstrating state change detection. A typical mistake is using a wider type unintentionally; ensure your declaration is uint8_t, not int, to see the wrapping behavior. After you complete the activity, reflect on whether the counter should wrap or whether the application needs a check to prevent wrapping. Counting 0 to 255 with uint8_t means implement and observe a uint8_t counter that wraps at 255 to learn how fixed-width types behave in practice.. In practical terms, a simple lab to observe wrap-around and practice the main loop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

#include <stdint.h>

int main(void) {
    uint8_t counter = 0;
    while (1) {
        // TODO: increment counter and add a short delay

  • counter wraps from 255 back to 0
  • a wrap event can trigger a state change like toggling an LED

Declaring counter as plain int may hide wrap-around; ensure you use uint8_t to intentionally observe wrapping.
Key Takeaway
This simple loop demonstrates how type choices directly determine runtime behavior; test and observe to build intuition.

screens.title: Compiling C for ARM Cortex-M
screens.subtitle: A minimal compilation workflow and what to verify

narration.text: Compiling for an ARM Cortex-M target turns your C source into machine instructions the processor executes. The workflow typically includes writing source files, invoking a cross-compiler configured for the target, and generating a binary or firmware image that can be flashed. In a learning environment you might use a simulator or an IDE that hides toolchain details, but the key checks remain the same: ensure your compiler target matches the Cortex-M architecture, include stdint. h for fixed-width types, and verify that startup code handles low-level initialization before main runs. After compilation, inspect the generated symbols or use the debugger to confirm that variables have the expected widths and that initialization ran once. A common confusion is assuming desktop build settings are valid for embedded targets; cross-compilation settings, linker scripts, and startup code differ. For a minimal embedded project, focus on correct compiler flags for the Cortex-M core and place peripheral initialization in the startup or early in main. The practical verification step is running the binary in a simulator or flashing it to a board and observing the expected behavior in the debugger or serial output.

keyIdea.title: Compile & verify
keyIdea.text: Target the correct Cortex-M variant, include fixed-width types, and verify initialization and type sizes using the debugger or simulator.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Compiling C for ARM Cortex-M
Minimal build checklist
  • Use a cross-compiler configured for your Cortex-M core.
  • Include stdint.h for fixed-width types.
  • Provide or use a startup routine that initializes hardware before main.
  • Use the debugger or simulator to inspect variable sizes and runtime behavior.
Verification
After building, load the binary in the debugger. Confirm that initializations run once and that variables have expected ranges. If using serial, print values to validate behavior.
Common pitfall
Using desktop compiler defaults can produce incorrect code for embedded targets. Always verify target flags and linker scripts for Cortex-M devices.
Key Takeaway
Match the compiler and linker configuration to the Cortex-M variant and verify runtime behavior in a debugger or simulator.

screens.title: Comments, formatting, and structured programs
screens.subtitle: Make firmware readable, maintainable, and auditable

narration.text: Readable and well-documented code is crucial for firmware longevity. Comments should explain intent and hardware-specific rationale, not restate obvious code. For example, comment why a particular mask is used for a hardware register rather than annotating every line. Consistent formatting — indentation, brace placement, and spacing — makes it easier to scan code during debugging or code reviews. Structure your program into small functions and handlers for initialization, periodic work, and event handling so each part is testable and understandable. Use meaningful names for constants, like LED_MASK or UART_BAUD, and prefer fixed-width types in declarations to make range explicit. A common misconception is that comments are optional in short projects; but firmware often outlives its original author, so clear comments and structure reduce bugs when code is extended. The practical habit to adopt: write a short header comment explaining the high-level purpose of a file and document any hardware assumptions you make so future maintainers know the constraints you relied upon. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Comments, formatting, and structure
Guidelines
  • Comment intent and hardware assumptions, not obvious code mechanics.
  • Use consistent formatting across files for readability in reviews and debugging.
  • Break code into small functions: init, loop body, handlers.
  • Name masks and constants clearly so bit operations read like sentences.
Example
Instead of commenting "set bit 2", name the mask and comment why that bit influences hardware mode, e.g., MODE_SELECT_MASK used to choose low-power peripheral state.
Why this matters
Firmware is frequently maintained by teams or revisited after months. Good comments and structure reduce debugging time and prevent regressions when engineers change hardware or features.
Key Takeaway
Invest time in clear comments and structure now to save hours of debugging later, especially for hardware-specific code and masks.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for reliable firmware

narration.text: Let's review three core concepts to retain. First, the embedded C program has an entry point and a perpetual main loop; initialization runs once and the loop performs ongoing tasks. Second, prefer fixed-width types from the standard header — uint8_t, int16_t, uint32_t — because they guarantee size and prevent portability surprises. Third, use bitwise operators with named masks to manipulate hardware registers safely, and be aware of unsigned wrap-around for arithmetic. Each of these points connects to a common practice: declare intent clearly through types and names, structure code for predictable runtime behavior, and document hardware-specific choices. These reminders should guide your next labs and code reviews. As you practice, check behavior in a debugger and verify that variable sizes and wrap-around events match your expectations. Persistent main loop

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three more compact rules to follow

narration.text: A few additional concise rules will help you avoid common embedded pitfalls. First, prefer the narrowest fixed-width type that safely contains the necessary range to conserve memory while remaining correct. Second, always document hardware-specific masks and register operations so that intent survives changes and reviews. Third, avoid blocking waits inside the main loop; use brief non-blocking checks, state machines, or sleep modes to keep responsiveness and power consumption under control. These micro-rules complement the earlier concepts and will serve as quick checks during development and code review. When you next write firmware, run a short checklist: are types explicit, are bit operations named and commented, and is the main loop free of long blocking calls? If yes, your code will be easier to reason about and more robust on different Cortex-M boards.

Keep the main loop responsive with non-blocking checks, state machines, or short sleeps.
